Profeasor Pet- ting played the organ and entertained the a.senibled guests with voluntaries oo the instrument previous to the arrival of the happy couple. The storm is over, but the agricultural wrecks (already alarming in IttlIlllyer) bestrew our lands— though not all, for many have yet to come. The magnitude of the disaster is overwhelming, and hitherto, in bur time, unequalled. I can number, in my own neighbourhood, many farmers who have lost from £2 to £6 per acre. Os our 47,000,000 of farmed acres the sum total must be fearful. irrespective of the landowners' losses loy unoccupied farms and diminished or unpaid rents. Happily there are some exceptional cases, and some of our northern friends have had special advantage., but as a whole, 1819 has been a cul- mination of agricultu-al ruin. Douglas, of 6, Iloward-place, Edinburgh, ints just patented an invention which seems to afford the means of obviating one of the most serious dangers connected with the corking of coal mines. It is well known that the protective efficacy of the Davy lamp teen often been rendered of too avail by the recklessness of miners, who would persist in taking off the wire-gauze top, either to obtain more light to work with, or to indulge in surreptitious smoking. The expedient of lucking the lamps has inovai ineffectual to prevent such miSCOISIOCE, novaus have been found for picking the simple locks emeoyed for that purpose. Me. Douglas, however, has devised an arrangement whereby any attemp to un.screw the top of the lantp must at once extinguish the light. His contrivance lA parpopelike, and can be adapted to any of the ordinary forms of the Davy lamp at present in use. To the under rim of the wire-game top he attaches a ratchet, made continuous round ito whole inner surface. A small toothed wheel is placed oto the oil yeses'', sore to fit into the ratchet whenever the two parts of the lamp am brought together., By meana of suitable gearing this wheel is made UP actuate, a spindle within the oil vessel, round which the inner end of the wick is roiled. When the top in screwed on, the toothed wheel is, of course, noode to revolve, but in this case with a motion contincsi to itself. Or the other hand, whenever the , process or unscrewing is commenced, and the wheel is con., sequently turned in the opposite direction, a clutch upon its axle comes into operation, with the result that the gearing in the oil vessel is brought into play, the spindle carrying the IVICIE being made to revolve in such Away as, to draw the ignited loortion down into the vessel, aml mains' guith the flame. So effectual is the working of the arrange- ment that the 1110111ent the unscrewing begno, the lighted portion of the wick commences to sink in its tube I And be- fore the lamp can be opened it has entirely disappeared, having, in fact, been drawn quite down among the oil. The mechanism is simple, and does not seem liable to get out of order ; and the expense of fitting it upon the orditmry lamp is mid to be comparatively trifling. The invention is. It is tr. -th;st the TX;;;;I;e—g;;;;;;Mient of Great Britain and Ireland is vestsd nominally in the Crown; hut practically in a committee of Ministers, commonly called the Cabinet, which has come to ateerli the function of the ancient Privy Council, or" the King in Council," the mem- ber, of whit:ll, bearing the title of Rigid lloneorekle, am sworn to advise the King according to the heat of their cunning and discretion," and to help and strengthen the execution of what shall bc resolved." Though not the off- spring of any formal election, the Cabinet is virtually ap- poinbed by Parliament, and more espeeially IT the House of 1 Commons, its existence being depeislent on the Tiossession of a majority in the latter as.mbly. As its :icts are liable to he quest imost in Parliament, and require prompt explamition,l Ito essential that the members of the Cabinet should have I seats in either the Upper or the Lower Rouse, where they become identified with the general policy and acts of the Government. The member of the Cabinet who fills the poaition of First Lord of the Treasury is the chief of the Ministry, and therefore of the Cabinet. It is at his recom- mendation that his colleagues are appointed ; and he di. penws, with hardly an exception, the patronage of the Crown. Every Cabinet includes the following nine mem- ber, of the Administration :—The First Lord of the Tom- tore, the Lord Chancellor, the Loot Powident .d the Coon- oil, the Chanced, of the Exchequer, and the five Seem- tari. of State. A number of other Ministerial functiona- ries, varying from two to eight, have usually seats in the Cabinet, th.e nowt frequently admitted being the Lord Privy Seal, the time Lord of the Admiralty, the President of the Board of Trade, the Viee-f°eeeidootof the Committee of Council on &location, the Postinaster-General, the Chief Secretary for Ireland, and the President of the Local Go- vernment Swint The ,election usually falls sport those amongst the last-mentioned functionaries whose rank, talents, reputation, and political weight render them the ' moat useful auxiliaries, or whom services, while in Opp.i- tion, may have created the strongest claims to become mem- bers of the Cabinet It has occasionally happened that a statesman poesessing high character and influence accepted a teat in the Cabinet without undertaking the labours and reeponsibilities of any particular office. Although the Cabinet has been regarded during several generations aft an essential part of the institutions of Great Britain, yet it motioner to be unknown to the law. The nom. of the members who compose it are cm er officially announced; no record is kept of its resolutions or meefings, nor has its existence been recognised by Act of Parliament—Sfoms- sion's

Some time ago I came across the following explontion of the letters on the four corners of wastage stamps, and it may perhaps meet the question of R.S.C., St. Helens. Theletters are pot there for the purpose of preventing pieces of two or more sbunps that have been used and obliterated from being joined together and made to do duty for new genuine stamps. The object is thus accomplishol:—:" A sheet of pennypostage labels as divided into twenty rows, each containing twelve . labels. The first row of twelve has in the top right hand and opposito left hand corners the letter "A," the second row of twe!ve has in similar positions the letter "B," the third o C," and no on to the twentieth now of twelve. The first row of twenty has the letter "A" in the top left hand and bottom right hand corners. the second now of twenty her the letter "B," the third "C," ano no on to the twelfth row. It will thus be .en that no two stamps ovary core sheet are inarkfd with the some letters, and also that the lower corners of each stamp contain the same letters as the top ones, but in an opposite position. Thus, a stamp marked "A " "B" on the top would allow the letters "B " "A" on the bottom. The irst and two following issues of postage labels simply had the letters in the lower owners, which did not prove. sufficient safeguard, and the present tn.le of marking—by which I believe the Bost Office is thoroughly protected— was introduced." Mr. Edward Cocker was the author of a over popular treatise on vulgar arithmetic, which went through upward, of 40 editions. His skill in caligraphy wan no less celebrated, he having published 14 different copy hooks, all entrraved with his own band. He was born in London in 1891. and died in 1677. Hence the phrase—"Acconling to Cocker." JAMES Earns, Warrington. Tike phrase, 'According to Cocker," is meant to represen accuracy in the science of numbers, particularly in that brooch which deals with accounts. Edward Cocker, lowborn the phrase owes its origin. was an adept in theart of engrav- ing, reciting, and arithmetic, and was lawn about the year 1831. Few traces of his handiwork in engraving and pen- i manship are now extant. His name is connected with his i "Arithmetic," a posthumous publication, issued by Hawkins, a brother writing-master in Southwark, in 1677, some time alter the author's death. Cocker's treatise is entitled, "A Plain and Familiar Method, suitable to lie meanest capacity, I for the full onderstanding of that incomparable art." lie I appear. to have entertained contempt for certain arithmeti- ! clans of his time. In his curious preface, he says, For you, ' the pretended numerists of this vapouring age, who are more disingenimudy witty to propound unnecessary questions than ingeniously judicious to resolve such to are neces.‘l7 ; ton, you w. this hook composed, it you will deny yourselves so much at to invert the streams of 'your ingenuity, and, by studiously conferring with the notes, names„ordersiProgres;. species, properties, proportions, powers, affections, awl applications of number., delivered herein, become such artiste, indeed, as you now only seem to be." 13.—Arnona BOREALIS, OR THE NORTHERN LIGHTS. M. T. W., Prereot, will fled that these lights, which are occasionally seen in the sky, are, by meteorologists, held to be a sign of an approaching magnetic stortn. Hallady re- gards the aurora ass magnetic phenomena, and his view is supported by Faraday. The simplest explaiution of there phenomena is"thattheyareno more nor less than the moisture in some shape (whether dew or vapour, liquid or frozen), illuminated by the heavenly bodies, either directly, or re- , fleeting their rays from the frozen masses around the Pole, or even from the immediately:approximate snow-clad earth." Hera, Warrington.

Philosophers are of different opinions as to the rause of the Aurora. It is, however, satisfactorily ascertained to he within the region of our atmosphere. Heli ascribed it to the reflection of the sun and moon by the clouds of snow and needles of Ice, which are constantly floating in the atmosphere of the frigid tones. Mairan supposed it to pro- from the atmosphere of the sun. Railly ascribed it to ! ' magnetism, and its remarkable influence on the needle har been generally observed. Biot. who was rent to the Shet- land Islands in 1817, by the French Academy of Sciences. to determine the length of the pendulum vibrating woods, had an opportunity—August 27 of the same year—of ob- serving the aurora borealis in all its splendour at the island of Dust. Oa this occasion he ascribed to the phenomenon a volcanic origin. His description is to be found in Blot's Pieces Elementaire de Physique. Die general opinion now- a-days is that the aurora is an electrical phenomenon and there is manifestly an intimate connection between it and the magnetism of the earth, as the magnetic needle is always greatly disturbed during a brilliant display of the aurora. Observations on this appearance were communicated by Richardson and Hood, in the appendix to Franklin's nar- rative of a Journey to the Shores of the Polar Sea, in 1819. by Roar, Parry, and others. A series also of interesting observations on a remarkable aurora, made in December, 1829, be the Rev. James Farguharson, of Alford, Aberdeen- shire, with an apparatus transmitted to him Iry the Royal Society of London will be found published in the transac- tions of that Society for 1830. N. • IThere are not wanting well-authentieated accounta in natural history of toads and of frogs being found in the I hearts of trees and in solid rocka, wholly enclosed and shut up from the air, deprived in all appearance of food, and Icing taken alive out of such situations ; an that the in- stance mentioned by Mr. Buckley, of Winsford, is not a solitary one. Ambrose Fare, chief surgeon to Henry king of France, relates thst he now come stones broken on his estate at Memlon, and that in the middle of a large, hard stone a huge live toad was found. There was no visible aperture by which it could have got there. In 1731 a toad was found in the heart of an oak tree at Santa. 'I here was no visible entrance t•, its habitation, and it was supposed that it must have been confined in the tree for nearly a hundred yearn. M. Hubert, professor of philomphy at Caen, relates that in the 1001 01 an elm, about the size of corpulent man. about 41t. above the root, and exactly in the centre, Wlln found a live toad, middle slued, hut lean, and filling up the whole vacant ,pace. As soon as a pamage was opened by the splitting of the wood, the toad mottled away very hastily. The tree was firm and sound. It wee eupposed that the egg from which the bud was formed must have lodged in the tree at its first growth, and that there the creature 'harl lived, without air. feeding on the inoistore and substance 01 11,0 tree. In 17900 Ilve frog was dug up at a distance 01 1111. from the sorface of the earth. In 1799, at Castletown, it a depth of five or six feet from the surface, many frogs. apparently inactive, and supposed to be dyed, were found. An "onus they were given air animation appeared, and they were found to be alive and healthy. In 1788, at a depth of 25 or 30 feet from the surface, a larg,e number of frogn were found, and on being exposed to the air they became active, but, unable to boor the rays of the can, most of them perished. Ala very early period the place had been a lake, and it was concluded that the frogs had been buried for many hundr•als of years, and that frogs placed in a situation in which they are perpetually supplied with moisture, and all waste front the body prevented, may preserve thz powers of life from age to age. On the 21st May, 1793, George Wilson, a mason, wantonly immured a toad inn stone wall he was building. In 1809—sixteen years afterwards—a part of the wall was taken down to make • weave for carts, and the poor creature was found alive in its stronghold. It was in a very torpid state, but soon recovered animation and activity, and, running to a collection of stones, disappeared. On the 2611, November, 1825, Dr. Buckland and some scientific friends placed a live toad in each of 24 cells—twelve in coarse limestone. and twelve in compact siliceous litnestone—with a double cover of glass and alqi of slate placed over each, and then cemented them down by a thin luting of clay. The stones were then buried at a depth of three feet, and remained unop,•tiol until the 10th of December, 1826. Every toad in the compact limestone was dead; the greater number in the porous lime- stone were alive. One had decreased in weight by 220 grains: one had increased its weight by 80 genius; another had Moment by 128 grains; and another bad decree/1.0274 grains. These were examined several times through the I glass cover, of the cells, but without removing them to admit air. They always appeared awake, and never in a state of torpor. Their meagreness increased at each inter- val at which they were examined, until at length they were found dead. Four other toads enclosed lean apple tree, which was made air-tight, were found dead at the end of a year. The works of Baptist Fulgoria Doge, of lien., and the famous physician., Agricola and Horatian, and Lord Verulam, treat of living toads found in very hard and entire atones. J. L. D., Sale.

..... - • Biths OF Sam—The law relating to Bills of Sale Is mainly contained in an Act passed in the year 1878, known as the .Bills of Sale Act:' This Act came into operation upon the let of January, 1879. One of the most important provisions was that which enacted that every bill of sale (which was executed after the lot of January, 1879) should be Signed and attested before a mlicitor. It in the duty of the solicitor to explain to the grantor of it (ere he signs it) the meaning of the document which he is about to execute. The intention of Parliament, of course, was by this enact- ment to put an end to the usury which has too often been exercised by money lenders over ignorant and needy persons whom they had induced to sign bills of nale. of the legal effect of which they were entirely ignorant when they ewe- , cu.d them. The other day Vice-Chancellor Matins laid it I down that the solicitor who witnessed the execution of a bill of sale must not be the money lender's solicitor. but leither the borroweee solicitor or an independent mlicitor called in for theespecial purpose of explaining the meaning lof the bill of sale to the grantor before he executed it. Every bill of sale must set forth the conaideration for which it has been granted. It niust alm be registered within seven days of its exert tion. If this be not done, the bill of sale will he void as against a trust. or aseignee in bankruptcy, sheriff's ! officer' and permns seizing in execution, Ac. There must, i too, be tiled with each bill of role, when it is registered, any schedule or inventory referred to in it, together with an affi- davit an to the time when the hill of sale was executed, and alma true copy of the bill of stk. If two hills of sa(taco given over the same goods they will—and this is very im- portant—hare priority in the oriter of the date of their regis- tration. The registration of a bill of sale (whether executed before or after the passing of the Bills of Sale Act, 1878) must be renewed every fire year., otherwise the registration will become of none effect. if, however. a Judge of the High Court of Justice is satisfied that the omission to register or re-register a bill of sale was accidental—or that any errors or omission, in it weno not wilful ones—he can order the till of sale to be reg,intered or re-registered, and the errors or omissions to be corrected. The evidence, however, neces- sary to induce a Judge of the High Court of Justice to that interfere must, wc. need hardy soy, be very cogent. The fee for registering a 101 l of sale is two shillings, and there in also a further fee of two shillings upon tiling the affidavit of execution. Any one can search the Reister of Bills of Sole tort fee of one shilling, and a mpy of'. bill of sale .n be obtained by anyom upon paying for it at the same rate as for office copies of judgments of the High Court of Juetice. It is not neconary to register a transfer or assignment of a bill of tale. Uusually a bill of sale contains a clause that the grantor of it will not remove th. goods from the houm If, however, he has done m (without the coneent of the grantee), the latter could put in force against him such remedies as are stipulated in the bill of sale itself. The holder of a bond ~fide bill of sale is in the position oft secured creditor, and may do one of three things—fa) If he given up his security he may prove for his whole debt , (Si if ho estimates its value he may prove for the balance (if any) or (r) if he chooses to realise it, he may prove for the deficiency (if ,any).

Count Moltke next addressed the House. He said : The mistrust of a nation for another is better removed by an understanding between Government and Government than by the Babel confusion of international brotherhood parliaments. All Governments wish M main- tain peace, and will maintain peace as long as they can Therefore a Govertunent must be strengthened, and not regarded ae a kind of hoatile power which cannot be sufficiently restricted. One must rather seek by all means to atrengthen and support the Government, for a weak Govern- ment is a misfortune to a country and a danger to its neighbours. It lea historical fact that the German Empire is a new State in Europe. All our neighbours are more or less safe from attack in the rear, and only need to present a frost on one side. They have stationGl a considerable portion of their land force close to our borders. Our regiments are distributed in equal proportions over the whole country. We nenl not seek for an intention in thin but we must take these circumstances into consideration. Before the Turkish war Russia began to extend in a con- eiderable degree her already powerful army, and since the conclusion has accomplished what she conimenced. Russia bas organised 21 new reserve division, of infantry and 24 reserve brigades of artillery, and she has supplemented 152 regiment, of infantry with a fourth battalion. France had formerly 28 divisions of infantry ; she has now 38. She had formerly 28 brigades of cavalry: she has now 3.5. The ! ntrength of the French army in its first mobilisation was ' formerly 338,000 men, whereas it is now 850,000. France has, therefore, doubled her army, while we have kept to the 1 per cent, of the population as fixed bean antiquated census. France has, at any rate, including the pen- I darmerie, which, however, belongs to the army, a force with Ohs colaurs of 497,000 nien, while Germany, with a popula- tion larger by several millions, has only 401,0110 men. The peace strength of Russia is twice as much as ours, namely, 8001100. The term of service in France is 20 years: in tins- sia 14: with an it is only 12. At the mune time we are in- yited to have thegenerositv to he the first to disarm. Has the German Michael ever drawn the sword except to protect his own skin P We cannot give a negative vote when the Government propories a moderate increase of our peeee strength in order that we may not remain quite behind our neighbours. Our neighbours in the west have not been able to bring themselves to decide upon a reduction of the term of crevice, but consider three years insufficient. In any case a more unfavourable moment for such a reduction could not be selected. I can only sincerely deplore that iron necessity compels an to impose fresh sacrifices on the Ger- man nation, but only through sacrifices and hard work havn! we agaM become a nation. During the decadence of the Imperial rule Germany wee the prise for which foreign powerxfought. The ruins on the Neckar and the Rhine are memonals of our bygone weakness. Who would forget that at the command of a foreigner Germans marched against Gennans ? We inust preserve and uphold peace abroad as faraa our stremgh allows. In this there is no threat hut a guar- ' antee for peace in our part el the werld, provided that we are strong and prepared for with weak forcee, with anus anticipating discharge, this end is not to be attained. EXECUTION OF KEAILNS AND BURN 3.

The execution of the two men, Hugh Burns and Patrick Kearns, for the murder of Patrick Tracer, at Widne,, on the 24th of October last, took place on Tuesday morning at Kirkdale Gaol. Liverpool. Mary Ann Tracey, the wife of the murdered our, ah.c convicted of the mine offence, being found by a jury of matrons quick with child at the tone of her convict., sentence Ir. respitc3 her case until after her confinement. No reporter. were admitted to witness the execu- ticn, the High Sheriff haring demanded the acquiescence I of the press in certain restrictions as to the publication of re- j porta, which were with accord repudiated. In accordance . veto a resolution of the visiting justice, however, the repre- sentatires of the press were allowed to enter the gaol pre- cincts in order to he present at the inquest, and it woe not unfit then that any infortnation regarding the execution was obtained.

That an execution took place within the precincts of Kirkdale Gaol was simply announced to the outer world by the hoisting of a black dag at 17 minutes after eight o'clock, hot whether one or two men. He hada 1., interview on the previous night with one of the prim eird officials of the gaol, and it wita no doubt, front the de- lade then received as to the stature of the unfortunate men, : that he bad, as he stated, made up his mind to give each of ! them "a drop of nine feet--a little more, or tnay be a little lens,'' according to b.c men way of putting the matter. Out- side the gaol, although snow and rain had been falling for more than an hour, covering the vicinity with a white pall twn or three inches in Villanelle, about 100 working men had congregated, mese at the... huddling innate:lv, together under the partial shelter of the north-west corner of the gad wall, while the remainder took to the open ground on per- pose to see the "black flag" hoisted. In this they were gratified, or they ought to have hem, becalm it was hoisted nest 3 minute or so before eight o'clock, probably to try whether it would run, and hauled down again, to hens. up a second time :is already stated, the prison bell tolling faintly in the meantime. Among the crowd were a few acquaintance of the doomed tnen from the neighbourhmd of Widnes, and one young man from Ireland, who had made the journey to see Kearns. but dun too late to obtain admis- sion. There could (icon certainty as tn who were prenatt at the execution, but it is clone th.it the high sheriff did not enMr the gaol between seven o'clock and 15 minutes past eight. --715;.iVidnes murder caused great excitement throughout Lincashire. and indeed the whole of England. It was one of those atrocioue outrages that niche the abhorrence of every civilised community, marked by a rool ernelty of predmadi- tation, a subtlety of arrmgenunt, and a shocking brutality of execution which were almost without a parallel among the many dark deeds of violence which have been committed of recent years. Thi. ehocking story of crime was epitomiaed in one sentence by Lord Coleridge, in sentendng the cul- prits, when he told them that they bad. crue:ly, deliberately, and ruthlessly—without any quarrel, without any kind of a .

extenuation Or excuse—mut'dered on unoffendingand nann- Ims man, front the basest awl wirl“xlost of all I,me and wicked motives." The evidence which brought this terrible crime home to the three culprit, was circumstantial, hat still the chain of circumetances wee on complete in every reapect—up to the most minete link—as to leave no reamon- able doubt in the minds of those Nil° hoard the case as to their. guilt. . . .

—The scsne dining the trial and at the sentence wee per- haps almost unexamplol in a court of justice. It was evi- dent the unhappy woman won in intense rein at times she would start up k 1 convulsively clutch the mils of the dock. But the other culprits were apparently unmoved, and although they cloady followed the evidence gave no sign of feeling thro,hout the trial. When Kearns statement was being read, Bares gave him a look of savage scorn When the verdict of guilty Wes found, Lord Coleridge delivered the dread sentence in the following awfully impressive terms After a patient investigation, and by the most righteous ver- dict, you have been found guilty of taking the life of a fel- low creature, and taking it cruelly, deliberately, and ruth- lessly. Without ant quarrel. without any kind of ion or or excuse, you have murdered a harmless and unoffend- ing man, from the basest and the wickedest of all hoae and wicked motives. For this awful crime it is not I who con- demn you. It is the law, whose minister I am, which says ttten you die. You sent your vietho out of this world hrto another without warning without a single moment of pre- paration. The law, in its sternest mood, is more merciful than you. You will hare that time which you denied. How you may stand now or hereafter beforo that awful Being, whose creatures we all are, it is not for one of the most sinful to presume. This only will I toll you as His WINIOM is infinite, tots His mercy unspeakable: INQUEST ON TIIE BODIES.

. --Ili:Ms-was-born in the county Carle, Ireland. After their conviction the culprits were attended by Father Bonte, the Roman Catholic chaplain to the gaol, who was most unremitting in his attennon to the unlmppy culprits. AN ORANGE "TEA EMIT" AT ST. HELENS. This week the Orangemen have had a meeting and have been "orating" at St. Helens, inn ball decorated in the usual s' glorious, pious, and immortal " fashion. The re- doubtable Mr. Touchstone was engaged to supply (ho speech of the evening, and, to do him justice. we may say he ap- pears to have diacharged the duty imposed upon loon in a fairly temperate manner, defending, no doubt to the best of his abilities, the home and foreign policy of the Govern. font. But the principal figure in the entertainment, the curiosity of the evening, was not Mr. Touchstone, hot the reverend " Chairman. This individual is described in our report am the Rev. Won. Carson, and he is no doubt a veteran member of the order-000 wioa is deeply imbued with its rampant militant spirit. Ate master of the kind of pothouse oratory, for which many Orange gatherings in the bad old times have been too often celebrated, commend on to this reverend brother ! His address, as reported, one sickening mixture of religious oretenaions, religious bigotry, vulgar abuse of eminent mem and all unelmriMbleness. We doubt

if amongst all the clergy of the Church of England any other lban an Orangeman could be found with the execrably bad taste to describe mie of the most eminent non of the time to thot despicable individual, William Ewart Glad- stone !" Jr it any wonder that the local church cler,v, Including even the Vicar of St. Helens, should Leg to be excused front attending o meeting that was to he presided over Ice Hideo' parson of a thoroughly rowdy type! From the confessions of Mr. Thompson, it seems that there was a strong feeling of flissatisfactionamongst the brethren on Tuesday night to the refusal of the local church clergy to attend their meeting. The excuses appear to have been nearly as multifarious as those made by the guests, who were bidden to tbe marriage feast, but as none of them could advance so potent a neuron for his absences. that he had married a wife, and, therefore, could not come, Orange- men at St Helens hove got into the doleful dumps with their whilom leaders.

ST. HELENS AND THE SIX VACANT SEATS. It was fully expected that the Chancellor of the Ex- chequer would have brought forward his Six Seats Bill on Thurnlav night, but for sorne reason he had promised not to to no after hall-pant eleven. The House being occupied in Committee until midnight, the proposal was not brought forward, and the War a general feeling of diaappointment amongst members. For some reason, tilE force of which we foil to see, time has been a general impression abroad that Accrington is to be one of the newly-enfranchised boroughs, but the London correepondent of a Liverpool paper, writing on Thursday night. contradicts this statement. Surely St. Helens, of which mention has not been recently made in connection with the vacant mats has a prior claim to almoet any other town in Englend. Previous to the passing of the Reform Bill in 1887, it was scheduled amongst the places entithal to be represented by one member, but for some reason or another was not included in the measure which came in force the following year. At that time it had a population amounting to about 45,000, and it has since been growing at a rapid rein in wealth and importance, and hoe now an estimated population of at leant 57,000. In fact, it is the most populous place in Lancaahire, and is the second on the lied of unrepresented towns, Croyden, near London, standing first, with a popula- tion of 71,315. The claims which Accrington can put forth to enfranchisement, are insignificant as compared with those of Be. Helens; the population in 1871 being only 21,000, and ita present estimated population about 30,000, or little more than half what it is at It. Helens. It it admitted on all sides that the county l'alatine is fairly entitled to it least one of the vacant scats, on the name principle that the seats taken from Ireland are to he restored to her. The almost decaying county town of Lancaster was very properly disfranchised for corropt practices, and, in order to adjust the displaced balance, enter or Lancashire is concerned the lievernin,nt could not do better than give a seat to the riaing and prosperous town of St. Helens, a very centre of several important in. doctrine.

div.head: EXAMINEE.
div.p: THE EXAMINEE.
SATURDAY, MARCH 6, 1880.
FARMERS AND SPORTSMEN.

It is notorious that the agrieulTural--Tisaa—ters of last year have made mauy farmers more discontented than ever they have been before, with the iujuriee nifficted on them by the over-preservation of game. The farmer, who is also a sportsman, may look with com- parative equanimity on the restruction of his turnips by hares or rabbits, or the injury to his fences and trampling of his crepe by dogs and horses. But the changes that are taking place in the conditions of modern English farming, make it in, on the man who han to makes living out of his own farm to dimourage this kind of thing at mach as possible. Even in the nutter of hunting there in in some comi- ties • species of secret war waged by farmers against the once favourite pastime, and wire forcer have been avowedly put up for the purpose of stopping it. Some two years ago hunting men were not a httie astonished and disgusted to find from a decision iv the Court of Appeal, that a field of horsemen follewing hounds in full cry had tot a right to ride anywhere and every- where. There are many arguments that could be adduced in favour of preserving the huntsman's privileges, but we fear that as it cannot he shown that foxes pay, or that hunting adds in any way to the profits of the agriculturixt, the glory of the old national sport must be on the wane. if indeed jibe doomed to ultimate extinction. What with rail- ways, wire fence“, the growth of the population and oonstant transformation of eras-al into urban districts, not to speak of poimuing of hounds and extermina• Son of foam, the huntenum of our day has difficulties to contend against that his father knew not oing of. And yet the injury inflicted on the farming clam by the huntsman and his hounds is but • small matter compared with what he suffers from the ravages to his crops by hares and rabbits. On this subject lively discussion took place in the 1-10nr,o of Commons on Tueeday night. The occasion was & resolution moved by Mr. Taylor, member for Leiceater, to the following effect :—"That in the opinion of this FlOll.BO the existing game law code maintained for the purpoee of preserving certain wild animals for vest, in unjust to the farmer, demoralising to the labourer, and injurious to the whole community, and should therefore be abolished." The Fo‘anetel Reform, Almonark, in its admirable analysis of the House of Commons, points out that more than two-thirds of the members are drawn from the laudocracy. Mr. Taylor's resolution was a remarkable one to bring forward for dincuseion in an ennembly so eonatitutad, seeing that it in for the most part composed of the very class for whose delectation the game laws have been framed and maintained up to the present hour. It is not likely under melt circuit...nem that • motion for the total abolition of these lawn would be seriously discussed, and, with the exception of the epeech of the mover of the resolution there wss an air of unreality about mom of what was said during Tues- day night's debate. On the whole, however, the opponents of the existing game laws and tlie suffering fanners have every reason to congratulate themselves en the result. Mr. Taylor delivered a most effective speech upon the whole subject, and a mom important admission was extorted from several quarters, and that went unchallenged, to the effect that great injury was done in many places to the farmer by the preserva- tion of an exeeseiee amount of ground g doe. This to maay will hen .elf-evident proposition, but it is some- thing behave the admit.un from a number of Tory landlords who are suppoeed to be such statuach friends to the farmers. Surely if they are se ready to admit that their "friends' are suffering so much injury from the ravages of ground game, the next step should be the adoption of measures that would enable farmers to protest their crops without violating the law.

We think with Mr. Taylor that it is most diwirable that previous to the general election the farming interest should understand clearly whet action their " friends" in Parliament ere prepared to take on this question. The game laws, h argues, are a queetion of enormous interest to the freemen. According to one hon. member, there have been a number of rases of i.olveut farmers in Norfolk whore ultimate run last yeue was attributable to the over preservation of game. They are laws that give • sanction to the old feudal principle of class

privilege, and there IA nothing like them in any other civilised country in the world. There are millions of scree in England alone sacrificed to game, and these shooting grounds are frequently adver- tised its being kept free of sheep. The member for Leicester, amid much laughter, instanced one plane that was recommended by an advertising agency as having an episcopal church in the vicinity, where a clergyman generally officiated '• in the *porting months," As an instance of the damage done to the farmers in this country by game, the case was mentioned of • valuer in Leicestershire allowing between £BOO and £9OO tonne tenant, or between twelve and thirteen pounds an acre, as compensation. The agricultural commiasioner of one of the London paper* recently related the case of a farmer whose root crops were so far consumed by hares that at length he wrote sarcastically to his

Red suggesting that he should send a load of turnips, otherwise his hares would starer 'Before the Christian era," says Mr. Taylor, • ` the Balearic islanders held the rabbit sacred. The animal was Or much worshipped now. The islanders being afflicted with a plague of rabbits sent to Rome for soldiers te, destroy them, the soldiers having no religious scruple. The Rome be wished to send to was the agricultural districts, and the soldiers he would engage were the enfranchised agricultural labourers." An amend- ment to the resolution, moved by Sir W. Barttelot that it was not now expedient to deal with the question, wse negatived without a division, and the resolution itself was thrown out by a majority of ;J. An amend-

Judging from the speech of the chairman at a Wesleyan Methodist home missionary meeting held at Runcorn, it seems that prosperous Christian Churches are tempted at times to look down from the sunny heights of success upon others who are not so fortunately situated. The chairman (Mr. John Siinpson) delivered a speech marked by consider- able originality of thought, in which he spoke of having noticed how easy it was, comparatively speaking, to get Christians to subscribe towards carrying on the work of foreign as opposed to Lome missions. lie paid a compliment to the St. Helens Wesleyan Methodist circuit for the hand- some .111 they had subscribed to the home mission fund—a circuit on whca that of St. Paul's, at Runcorn, were at times tempted to look down with contempt. Let as hope that the members of St. Paul's circuit will try to "walk humbly," for spiritual pride is nost strongly condemned by all scriptural writer..

Mr. Thom., Norman, of Runcorn, seeme to be no busy with ether matters that he has no time to devote to the question of public baths. or can it be that the scheme has been consigned to the limbo of forgotten things? It wee I generally thought that Mr. Norman would not have been no easily eneffed out by the ridicule of a few gentlemen oppmed to the measure. I hope there ie no truth in the rumour I heard the other day that the intraluction of the scheme to the puhlk of Runcorn just before the election was the trick of cue who is "an old campaigner." Philip Speakman proposed that an honorarium of 1.50 ehould be given to the directors for their services during the last ;ten years, and Mr Thomas Norman nolemnly suggested that £lOO should be handed to the gentlemen. It is plmeing to see that .Mr. llrundrit, who occupied the chair, and him tellow-directors did not encourage such a singular proposal, when I believe this is the only half-yearly meeting since the formation of the company tbat dividend has been paid. It is hardly a (lllle to receive rifts when people who have had money in a concern for so nany years have never had a penny of dividend for their bcked up funds. Mr. Philip Speakman has given notice of a very tmportant notion for consideration at the next meeting 01 01.0 Runcorn Inprovement CAnnissioners, •ir., of a proposal to purcham tha prorwrty of the Runcorn, Weston, and Halton Water- works Company. 'lite suggestion i, 3 valuable one, for it is quite evident that if, as the years progrese, the shareholdere of the company tind that tney obtain a good per tentage for their money, they will be disinclined to sell the works at anything but an exorbitant price. Widnes, and various other eurrounding town', have the waterworks in the respective .ploces in their own hand, and some of them are making a gnod profit, which goes to the reduction of the rater. It is to be regretted that the motion should be brought forward by a gentleman who bolds stock in the company, an it is not at all improbable that those who are oppoeed to the pur- chase will not be inclined to view it with any additional farvour because it is brought forward by a gentleman who am, elk.ck in the concern.

div.head: CLEVER CAPTURE OF THE ABSCONDING WIDNES RELIEVING OFFICER.
div.p: CLEVER CAPTURE OF THE ABSCOND- ING WIDNES RELIEVING OFFICER.

Much excitement was caused in Widnes yesterday morn- ing by the announcement that Anther Fowler, who formerly acted as relieving officer to the Prescot Board of Guardians, and absconded about six months ago, had been captured in London by Inspector Barnett and brought to the lockup at a late hour ott the previous night. A short time ago • p sat- graph appeared in a Liverpool paper—for the truth of which we cannot vouch—to the effect that an attempt had been made to secure the runaway by one of the Widnm police force, but it had failed. This annourcement was scarcely believed in the town until a report became circulated that, J instead of Fowler being across the Atlantic ocean, he was in the metropolis, and in conamunication with his wife. It was I said that he had forwarded her some money. and his wife, I with an extraordinary degrm of carelessness, had sent d daughter of somewhat tender years to post a letter in reply J at a pillar-hos some distance from wlaere she was stayin,i, j and that whilst going the jonrney tbe child lost the missive ;anal cried no bitterly in anticipation of punishment that the • attention of a crowd of people was called to the occurrence. ! Shortly after, Mrs. Fowler herself was seen seeking the j letter, which had in the meantime been found by a gentle- ' mint dot taken to tbe police, who in tide manner obtained the addrem of the unfortunate rascal.

line circumstances attending the disappearance of the ' officer may have been forgotten by many of our readers. They may be briefly ShlhAl as follows —On Saturday,the 23n1 August, on the floe people in the district over which Fowler toed control in Widnes—he residing at Simms Cross, and also acting AA registrar of marriages—going to receive their usual pay, it W. found that he faikl to put in appearyce. Several weary hours were allowed to pass in the belief that had login delayed on some other business. Enquiries wore at once made, but nothing could be found out except that he had not been moon in the town since noon of the previous day, when it was Fowler's custom to each the cheque from Mr. Hartley. the clerk of the Guardians It was, however, very soon discovered that the relieving officer had cashed the cloque on the Wedneslay, and, we need Inanity oily, abwonded. Happening atm near a date to the disappearance of Mr. l'ierce, the accountant to the Widnes Local Board, the absconding of Fowler caused quite a sensation. We believe we are correct in statingthat an officer was despatched for the porporw of finding out The whereatiouta of the fellow; but he came back after et fruittess chase, and this is not to be wondered at if the statement %ince sand to have been made by bowler is correct, {IOW he ionnegliatel, shipped to Africa in one of Messrs. Donald Carle and Cot chips. The police were aware of the fact that the absconding official hail in his youth been a sailor, and they seem to have been of opinion that if he were found anywhere it would either bene board some veasel or working in One London docks. The detectives at Scotland Yard were provided with a mull description of the nitnaway, bat they were not able to meet with him. The Widnes police were, of course, a little chagrined that the bird NA escaped, and Superintendent Brindle appears to have determined to put the clatter into the bands of hie deputy Inspector Barnett, whose effurts in gathering the evidence necessary to obtain a conviction in the late murder case proved so successful. The result proves that the choice was well made, as when the Inspector returned, he brought the wanderer home with him. It is gated that the hive, tor disguised himself on getting to the metropolis, and at once put himself in communication with the detectives at Scotland Yard. Inquiries resulted in the discovery that the ex-relieving officer WOO working at the docks, and lodging at Poplar. On Tuesday ereoing Fowler was seen by the In- spector to enter the house whore Inc usually lodged, at.d it was determined that a ree g should he employed in attempt- ing his capture, as he was known to be remarkably fleet of foot. The officer got aosist.ce and Jetermined to surround the lionise after the inmates had retirod to rsst. Thia plan Wan carriegl out at about one o'clock on Wednesday morn- ing. One of the inen went to the door and, after considerable rapping, got a hearing from the landlady, who, how ever,oras only constrained to open it on the representedott that aome- thing very seriouo had happened in the immediate neigh. boyhood, and assigance sras imperatively needed. The woman fell into this snare, and poor Fowler was the first man who ran out of the house. He found a reception in the strong arms of the Inspector, whom at the first he did not reoognise in hia disguise, and coolly asktsi °what was up." On bsing salutea with tine words ° Well, Arthur," in tine woll known tones of One inspector for the Widnes divi- -Biog With whom, of comae, he ciao remarkably well acquainted owing to baying to frequently to appear at court as prosecutor against absconding husbands, Inc completely collapsed. Fowler was Mken to one of the London police stations, and removed to Widnes on Thurslay, where he arrived late itt night. When apprehended, the prisoner stated that since his diappearance he had tgen to Africa, and he was thoroughly diagoged with hienself for not accepting the offer made to him of 78. 61. per day "and all found," whilot in that country. Yesterday morning he was was brought before Mr. F. Gossage, at the Widnes Police Court, which waft quite deserted, although the principal door was open to the public. The only people present were the representatives of the press, Mr. Lewin, deputy magistrates' clerk, and the police. The prisoner app..ared very bronsed, ant more a serge jacket. He wax rather nervous, kept his eye, down, and appeared heartily it.sharned of his position. Inspector Barnett said the prisoner was chmfred with em- bessling the sum of £25. the moneys of the Preseot Board of Guardians, on the 230,1 August. A warrant wee taken out at the time, but before it could be oxecuted he die- appeare.L He briefly related the principal details of the apprehension, and asked horn reinand, AO that he might communicate witlt Mn. Hartley, the clerk to the Prescot Board of Guardians, and other gentlemen interested in dm Mr. Lewin read over the warrant to the prisoner, and the Inspector maid he had done the wile at the time of the ap- prehenition, but the prisoner made no answer. Prisoner asked that he might stay at Widnes during the time of the remand, but Inspector Barnett said he could not consent to such e request beMg granted. " .
M. (.go said the prisoner would be remanded until the 12th inst.

liuring tile comae of the afternoon the prisoner was no. moved to KirkdliC Gaol, and as he pass.sl down Victoria- rood in the company of Inspector Harnett, to whom the greatest credit is due for the capture, we need hardly say I that he was the observed of all observer, and a large crowd followed. Prisoner was dressed in a long overcoat, and walked with a color step. fie was taken to Kirkdale by the , London and North-Western flailway Company's line.
THE CHARGE AGAINST A WIDNES -,VOMAN FOR DEFRAUDING A AIONEY-LENDER.

I Sarah Lewis, a woman residing at Terrace-row, Widnes, wan charged at the Manchester City Splice Court, with obtaining money by false and fraudidelt pretence. Mr. Bradbury, barrisferod-law appeared to prosecute, and Mr. Harris for the prisoner. Mr. Bradbury stated tint James Townend, the prosemdor, wars money-lender carrying on business in Mancherter, and during the month of March lard the prisoner arranged with him for the loan of £B, the security being the household furniture belonging to her husband. It waa arranged that a bill of sale on the furni- tura should begiven, and when the negotiations were con- cluded Mr. Townend's clerk told her that her husband must come to the prosecutor's office in Manhcester to sign the bill of sale, and that a cheque would then be given him for the amount. Accordingly on the Bth Aped last year the prisoner and a man presented thermelves at Mr. I Towneuars efface in Brazennose-street. Mr. Townend tsked the menuf he was Mr. James Lewis, and before lie had time to reply the prisoner raid, "Yen ; heir my linstand." The ,tailtit sale was then executed, the man present signing it ' "James Lewis,' and a cheque for £8 was handul to him. The cheque was presented and mid at the bank, It subs, quently turned nut that the whole thing was a fraud, the man who signed the bill of rate not being the pri- soner's husband at all, but an entire stranger to her. Detective Inspector Tote apprehended the prisoner at Widnes under a warrant. and charged her with obtaining money from Mr. Townend by false pretences. She replied, "t did receive the money, and I will tell you the man's name; it is William Lown'cle. and he lives at 70. Cametery-road, Runcorn. I gave him ss. and paid his railway fare from Widnes to Manchester, and he said it would be all right."--James Townend said he was a money lender and carried on business at 25, Brazen..., street. Stanchest°, In March hod year he received an ap. plication for the loan of £B, and after some correspondence and after hie clerk had visited the prisoner's house in Terrace-row. Widnes, the arrangements for the loan were concluded. On the Bth April following the prisoner and a man came to hie office. He asked the man if he was Mr. James Lewir, and the prisoner replied, "Von, he is my husband.' Wanesc tnade out the bill of sale produced, and the man signed it " James Lewis." He then gave him a cheque for £B. He parted with the <berme believing the man was Jas. Lewis.— . William Ciapperton, 3 clerk in the employ of Mr. Townend, gave evidence as to his going to Widnes to see the furni- ture.and to make the necessary arrangements for the loan. The money waste be repaid in fortnightly instalments of ss. Some insmlinenm were paid. hot one being unpaid he went to Widnes to enquire about it,taking a man with him to seize the furniture if necessary. He saw the prisoner, who made some excuse for not paying the instalment, and said she could not pay it that day. She added that her husband was working at St. Helen. and would not be home until the end of the week. Witneee told her she must fetch her husband or pay the instalment, otherwise he would remove the goods. She then went away and fetched her husband, who was working at soMe place in Widnes. Before leaving the house to fetch him, Ale said "I may as well tell you the truth : my husband knows nothing at all about it.” When the husband came he expressed his surprise in a very strong manner .indeed at her having done such a thing. The husband sant he had been in the habit of giving her .E 2 a week to keep the house, that they had no children, and that she had no business to borrow money—This was the rare for the pro...Minn.—Mr. Harris , said that the prisoner's husband was now willing to assume the reeponsibility and pay the money, and he hoped the magistrates would deal with the caw. The husband tenet' highly respectable man and had lived at trwlem for the last 18 yearn—Mr. Headlam said it wane case in which he had no jurisdiction: it must go to the Sessions.—Mr. Harris said he was under the impression that the magistrates could deal with the cam under the new Summary Jurisdiction Act.— Mr. Headlani : No, I cannot.—The prisoner was then com- mitted for trial at the next City Seirsione.—She wee ad- , mitted to bail in two eureties of £:10 each.

div.p: STRANGE CHARGE AGAINST A WIDNES LADY.

- -• Mrs. Sarah Ann Farrant, of AO, Terrace-road, the wife of Mr. Farrant, junr., or the firm of Messrs. Farrant and Son, Waterloo-road, Widnes!, and whose first husband was Mr. Richmdson, butcher, formerly of Widnes, was charged, on remand, with having, on the 10th December, 18714, stolen a flannel singlet, two holland apraus. two pairs of drawers, A night dress, three pillow slips, a window curtain, a dress jacket, four glasses, a large meat dish, a plate, and 13 pawn, tickets, value ES 10, the anode and chattels of Mr. James Lewis, bricklayer, of 106, Terrace-road, tiIAA town. Mr. kkaeley defended. Mr. Lewin, deputy magistrates' clerk, explained to the Bench that at the last court the bearing of tae case mminst the defendant was adjourned, in consequence of a with to that effect baying being expressed by the proaecutor's wife, who wee not present that day owing to having been appre- hended at Manchester and committed fortrial on a charge of obhtining money under false pretences.

Mr. 13;asley ;aid that in thre absence of any evidence, he should certainly ask for the dismissal of the summons against his client. The prosecutor stated that be should like tbe case to be aajourned, as his wife was, of course, unable to appear under the circumstances.

I Mr. Beasley sa-tid that if the proseentor's wife bad thought , it necessary to go on with the charge. she could have been I brought there. 11 Prosecutor sa.l the defendant had been lodging at his : house fore more than twelve months—he could wit give the , precise date. He believed it would lieu year and a half I since she came to live there. She left just before Christ- mos. Before she did so his wife was away from home, and as he suspected that some of the thing, were being removed . from he hcuse, lie sem word to her. to return. Amongst the , articles taken were those which the defendant was chargert with stealing. Ile never gave the defendant liberty to take the things, nor did he evtr tell hie wife she might grant per- mission to sue one to to se. Amongst the articles remove! , were his gold watch and chain, Whiell were worth LP, and the lather goods about El in value. Ile missed the things after I ths defendant left.

Cross-examined by Mr. Beasley Defendant was a widow at the titne she first mule to hi., house, and she rented some rooms of him, and furnished them ',emelt. He believed that it woe quite correct that hist wife went to Manchester and forged hie natne toe bill of sale. It. believed she had been com- mitted for trial on the charge of obmining a sum of Lire, £lO from • loan eociety. tie knew nothing about the bans- action personally, but he had been told that the money woe obtained after a nom had come from Manchester and inspecteu his furniture—not the furniture which the def,ndant had in the rooms she had taken from him. The bailiffs came to his house front a motley lender in Mar cheater in the inonth of October. Ile was at that time ahowo a bill of sale, and the permn holding it threatened to sell hie things up, but he ex- plained that he knew nothing at all about it. The defen- dant had the bailiffs in her own ruonis all the night and though he woe actually at the house at the time. he was not aware of this until afterwards. He did Mt know that the bailiffs seised any of the defendant's goods for the debt. 10 was not correct that he sent his wife away in order to pre- vent her being tweeted for what she had done. His wife was away nine or ten weeks, but lie did not know why she remained all that time. Ile could not say that lie had ever consulted a man known as " Lord t haff," but he had written hini (witness) one or two letters. One of these had been sett to the defendant, and another to her mother, upon his (witnesalt) instructiona. This took place at the begin- ning of last month. 'Ulm auto of £2 was not got from the defendant to enable hi, wife to go away without las know- ledge—at least, be had no knowledge of this. Defendant remained in the [tense about two months after his wife went , away. Ile believed his wife first went to Wolverhampton, I and then to Shropshire. the dill not know who provided I her with money logo, lint since she bad returned she hon told him that the defendant'a mother gave her .£2 "00 go out of the neighloo•rhood, in order to keep the matterquiet." He had not been told by the defendaM that she bestowed the £2 of her mother in order that his wife might go away. Defendant never told him at the mine time that his wife had given her the pawn tickets as a security for the debt. I He could not say whether the note produced was make handwriting of " Lord Chaff "—(laughter)—as he was no scholar ; but he was quite aware that that ',emu wrote a note on the mute date—the 10th of February. He did not write the note for the purpose of frightening the defendant, but all lie wanted at the little was to get he things back. His object was certainly not to extort money from the de. fendant. 'The matter was not talked over between him and land Chaff." and it was never propoeed that they ahould : get mine money out of defendant by having her arrested. He did not know that the mother of the defendant was able to live in an independent condition, as lie had never had anything 10 110 with her. Vrosecutor again applied for an adjournment. Mr. Ilmaley contended that he had proved enough by his cross-examination to show that the charge preferred against his client was perfectly groundless. How could the magistrates come to the conclusion that the things were stolen when at least two of the lowa tickets were for two of the very same articles as the defendant was charged with stealing. PROPOSED sciwoi. BOARD FOR WARRINGTON.

'rho MATO@ : The next 'object ith.t 1111 Ch Will be moved by Councillor Milner:—.That this Council forthwith makea application tho Education Department to canee a School Board to be formed for dna borough, and that the Town k take. all necessary stepa to give effect to this resolo- .. .

atm. Councillor MILNER said : In rising Co move this motion I I feel I am taking a somewhat serious step, but it is one that bat presses' no much on my mind since the pa.ing of the Education Act, in 1870, that I feel that I could not any longer defer taking some steps at any rats to test what the feeling of my fellow townsnien wes in regard to this Act. Education has taken a very different position since the , passing of the Act of 1870. to what it did before that time; it was generally felt that it was needful to have education, I and that the people should be educated. But until that Act was passed I am not aware that any English Ave lays it down ax the duty of the State to provide e location for the people. Since that time there bad been another Act of 1873, which really makes it a criminal net of any parent who withholds education from his children. That has been again supplemented by the Factory Are, which declares that no chill shall go to work until it is 13 years of age, and hen tamed what is known as the 4th standard of the Educ. don Code. Now this being the easel anyof opinion that the education nrovided in Warrington is deplorably insuffi- cient. In 18701 wantol very much the gentlemen who were then in this Council to take steps for the formation of a Board. , I wanted to see Warrington taking the same position in: regard to this Act that was taken in regard to the Fr., Libraries Act. Warrington was the fir+t town in England to adopt that Act; and I ilo not think that any Act of this Cor- poration has ever given more satisfaction to the ratepayers of the town. I should have liked very much 1,, have seen the education queetion treated in the same way ; but, unfor- tunately for the Act twing adopted. Warrington had been rather ahead of the rest of England, up to that time, in elementary education, and it was not considered advisable to throw the tows at that time into the heat of a contested election on this question, which was then exciting a good deal of angry feeling all over the country. The opportunity went by, and I would remind you since that time .other generation has grown up and gone out into the world not half educated, not half fitted, to fight against the difficulties of this nineteenth century life. It was urged at the time that a vat antary effort would supply all the school ammo- lesion that was needed, and terry great effort was made both then and sines to do it. I think no praise can be given .fficiently high to those gentlemen who made the attempt ' to lack up their conviction, that voluntary effort could I supply the needful educttion, and from that time have dem all that they could to supply Warrington with the needful accommodation. So has as accommodation is concerned they have done it. I have no h.itation in saying that I have not moved this motion to-night because their is a lack of seats in the schools of the town, but because the education given is not up to the mark. (Hear, hear.) I want just to say afro, words why I think the voluntary effort hoe and oast fail. You gets committee of men who are most earnest and desirous to do certain work. For a thne they work together, but they have no formal obligation to stick Co the work, and first one drops a little off, and another drops • little off, money becomen difficult a get in. and the thing is not a success. There are constant improvements and altera- tions wanted in the schools, additions to the hooka, and what not and every onset theec has afresh call on the liberality of the few gentlemen constituting the committee— very often a call on the tr.surer or the secretary. There are gentlemen I know sitting round this hoard who could if they only ohone to speak—l know they won't and never will—hut if they chose to speak they could give , an account which .cull very much astonish the inhabit.. of Warrington to know whom they are indebted to for the elementary education of the town. (Hear, hear.) There are secretaries of elementary schools round this table who have had to pay bill, year after year in a way which I think in disgraceful to the rest of the inhabitants. And then again in regard to the voluntary effort I .nnot di...Gate front my mind the feeling that education which depends upon the charity of individuals is degrading. I believe the right of education is the right of everyone born ' in a civilised state, and that everyone living in the com- munity ought to contribute to thegeneral good of the whole in the matter of educe:. m. just as much an we contribute to making roads round the, town. providing the town with gas, and a supply of water—just in the manner then we ought to supply education. Now a few reasons why I wish for a School Board. Eirat. that the cost of the schools will be equally distributed over the community. Then again, that the educatioq given in Board schools is better. I will give the reason for that presently that the attendance in shoool beanie is better ; that it is cheaper than voluntary achon,s,, especially if graded who°te are adopted. By “gnuled schools I mean this the edueotion given in inspected 1 schools is divided into six standanla. If instead of having the standards in every school in the town we had seprate , schools with the two :lowest in one Behold, the two next another, and the two next in another, the time and atten- tion of the head master instead of being frittered away over young children would be given to more advanced students, and the result would be in every we more satiefactory Now, an immense amount of time is diverted Prom the better. education of the children by bulking after those who are young, and the teaching of the different standards in the same school produces confusion and anything but eatisf ic- tory results. I have mentioned dready the requirements of the Feeney Act at another reason for having a .Ichool Board, and then a paragraph OCCIII, in the last Blue' Book,l containing the report of the Duke of t Richmond and Lord I Bandon. to which I would call the attention of everyone in- terested in the maintenance of voluntary schools, because this paragraph pute their future in a very serious light. l'he report nays--" The annual Government granes to eh, mentary achonle rose in the year trots £1,548,3231 to £1,820481. or from 14s. 4FI. to lbs. tj.l. per I scholar in average attendance • while the grant. for the current financial year is estimated at 15e. Dd. per head. We think the time hat come when it will have to be considered whether it is necessary to maintain 1 this high rate of aid for the future. now that the operation of the bylaws has la,ely added to the oninber of our acholars, and has enabled so many of them to earn for their schools grants, of which a large proportion (nearly two- fifths) is paid merely in respect of their enforced attendance. It Is to be borne in mind that the heeling condition. on which the Parliamentary grant is now administered were settled before the effect of compulsory edumtion had been or any reliable .tirnate could be formed of the profitable results of the working of this new system." this means that the grant which they state is 15s. 3d. per bead, will his seriously reduced, and if that amount is reduced I do not sm how voluntary schoole are going Co be conducted at all. because in Warrington thme are very few schools which are not in debt. or. if not in debt, have only Ina 6.111 relieved from debt by some special effort on the part of some ' few gentlemen in the town. With reference to the number of Board schools in England, there are 13 towns of over 100.000 inhabitants, and all of these have School Boards. There arc 21 towns with over 50,000 and less than 100,0001 inhabitants, end all have School Boards but Preston 02 towns with a population under 50,000, 47 of which have Sch., B.rds, and V have not and I am sorry to say that we stand in the latter use. During the year far which this Blue Book was publabot —and on which I have all the statistics I make use of —there were three more school Boards formed than in 1878, and no such Boards were dis- aolved during that year. I should like to call Mr. Kean'.

RAILWAY LINE EXTENSION NILL/I Sr. Hslans.—We see happy to hr able to state that some of the long-standing railway grievances of this district have been removed by the opening of a new line of rails of about a mile in length, con- necting the Sutton to Black Brook line with the Lancashire Union line near the Carr Mill Dam. This connection will divert the greater part of the heavy mineral traffic from the Wigan coal fields for sl idnes and Liarston Dock, thereby giving considerable relief to St. Helens Station. 'The work of cutting and exicuting this new branch was entrusted to Mr. Nowell, of Manchester, according to plans furnished be the company's own engineer. This has been very eatisfaC- torily done, the line being opened on the 2nl ult., a few tnonths after the commencement of the work. The line is not intended for pissenger traffic at present, but for minerals and goals exclusively; and in addition to relieving the crowded traffic through St. Helens it also affords a shorter route for the mineral train.. The wonder is that this relief hae not been attempted sooner considering the difficulties the company have experienced in carrying each an enor- mous quantity of traffic through St. Ilelens Station, where the pasisetiger traffic is also very heavy. For some time back unpunctuality of the train eervice and the frequent die- appointments to business people have been very seriously Intl and the marvel is that ea few iicoiderta should have occurred while such a state of things existed. Whilst the travelling public in this district congratulate themselves on the proepect there vomit greater punctuality and .gene- rally improved service of trains, they will, no doubt, at the mote time pay their tribute of praise to the officers of the line, who under the gre&te,t difficultim did all they could and succeriled in working tie traffic without any serious canaltba.

Dr. Sephton nocu pied the chair. We think we may fairly congratulate the corn- miller on having on this occasion eclipsed their previooa efforts, the musical fare being such as is not often provided at a country concert. When we mention that the programme , included the names of the Misses Horton, Richardson, and of Memrs. Bellian. Parr, and Reddish, it is needless for an to say anything as to their performances other than they rendered their mngs in a pleasing and effective manner and fully sustained their Warrington reputation. The committee had been fortunate enough to obtain the services of Mr. 11. F. William; of Liverpool', who was evidently the favourite of the evening. SINOTIAIi ACCIDENT AT GOLBONNE STATION.—At borne Station, on Wednesday morning, an ordinary four- wheeled passenger'c luggatre truck used at the mention was blown on to the main line from the platfarm. A light engine proceeding to Earlestown in order to convey the night mail passed through the station About 2-39. and speedily removed : the obstacle, c,,rnpletely smashing it to piece, and matter- ing the fragments about the line. The driver was somewhat alarmed, and returned to the station in order to ascertain the I state of affairs. Finding what had occurred, he quietly col- ! tented the .shatters" together, placed them inn beep on the ' platform, and proceeded on toe journey. SNOWS OF SoNO.---A service of tittered song, entitled • 'The Life of Moses," was given in the Congregational , Church on Sunday afternoon by the choir and members of , the Sabbath school in comoTOoct with the church. The at. tendance was very goml, the church being nicely filled. Tn. Rev. David Young, 8.A., paator conducted the service, which was opened with an appropriate hymn. followed by prayer. The `. Bible Story, which is one of I'. K. Longbot, ! tom's, was an intereating and pithy account of the various stages in the history of Moses. The mush,' portMn wee well adapted to the various sceees. The ohject of the ser- vice was to raise funds to replenish the school library. The afternoon'e offerings realised £6, which together with the amount previously collected gives £8 5s 5,1 towards the deaired object. Metiers to Ott fittor.

shall feel obliged if you will kindly insert a few lines on the abovesubject. Doubtless you are aware the the desirability of running Sunday trains Boni ht. Helens has been advocated for some time. Atone time a memorial to the Lon- don and North-Western board of directors was thought of. Now, every one residing in ht. Helens and continually inhaling the vitiated air of the place, loaded with all kinds of impurity thrown off from chemical works and other manufactories, must admit the necessity of facilities being given to the inhabitants to obtain an occasional change of air. Now it is only im Sundays that small struggling tradespeople and the great mass id the working classes can leave the town, and they are in a great irmsure prevented from having their Sunday out because there is so poor a train service. Why should we not have a mid-day service as well as people residing at Itaintaill. Horton, Sc.? Here is a town of 50,000 or 00.000 of population domed the privilege con- ceded to places of secondary importance. I believe that site present trains could be utilised so as to meet the wants at ht. Helene, and that if the company were only asked to consider thesubject at once they would do so. It would be felt as a great boon if people could run down to Liverpool early after dinner and return about 8.30, tone to give them a chance of visit- , ing New Brighton or other resorts, or to attend evening serrice at one or other of the Liverpool churches or chapels, 1 if so inclined.—Yours, oho., A TRAVELLER.

Str,—Your impression of Saturday last contains another contribution from the pen of "BaMenge." Not being com- petent to debate the relative merits of arbitration and strikes, at means of settling questions of wages in the iron trade, " Balltongs." to ease his mind, must needs go out of his way to misrepresent and abuse me for haring committed the very serious double offence of visiting Warrington and re- ceiving the little salary voted to me for services rendered in the office to which I was appointed by some thousands of my fell.iw-workinen. If " Balltongs "in entitled to nothing more, he is certainly entitled to some credit for having ex- preased an opinion of my situation and services no widely different to the opinion so generally expressed by the Rte. mixylum Poet, Midlan,ll'euntie, Lcpnv. and other leading impartial organs. But in all trnotability Balltange " con- siders himself not only the most competent judge. but also the fairest critic. The statement that I once tried to do something and failed I pass by. The statement that I made a claim to ss. and only got Is 64, can be met by the state- ment that "Balltongs" did not make any clahn or get any- thing at all. It is quite true that during the late depreseion in trade many ironworkers—l fear. &idly too many—were reduced tot state of semi-starvation and if " Balltongs thought more of that sad fact he would not advise working- men to have nothing to do with baards of arbitrrion. I would here o:Aferve that surely Tuy receiving isome £2 per week was not the cause of the depression. I will venture to suggest to Balltongs- that the late depression in trade was the result of a combination of causes over which neither I myself nor my pay could possibly ex- ercise the least control. The several bad harvests since 1871. the late famines in India and China, over-production. foreign competition, and the decennial cycle which it is said has been going on for the last 150 years, may have been important factors ,if the late trade depression. From these or other canoes the English iron trade has suffered quite sufficient without the suffering being intensified by such agencies as strikes and lock-outs. But to reason with Balltongs " in this way, I take it, is about on a par with offering Balam strawberries. Therefore, I will conclude this correspondenceeo for oaf am concerned. by giviry; the would-be peraclate of the Warrington ironworkers net this little piece of advice. riz.:—That if he has the least desire: to put his conscience on a peace footing. he must first place hia pen and tongue on the civil list. All being well I /Mai I visit Warrington again is a short time. when I shall be pleased to meet "Italltongs" in person, and then we might be able to reconcile the little differences in opinion existing ' between us.—Vours respectful lv,
JAMES CAPPER, Operative Secretary Staffordshire Iron Trade Board of Arbitration. Walsall, March 3, 1880.
